question: What is the primary physiological disadvantage associated with the oral route of drug administration?

options.C: High risk of local skin infection

explanation: Drugs absorbed from the gut enter the portal circulation and pass through the liver, where enzymes can significantly reduce the active drug concentration before it reaches the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: A patient scheduled for oral medication administration has been vomiting continuously for the past four hours. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Force the patient to drink water to settle the stomach
options.B: Crush the medication and mix it with fruit juice
options.C: Withhold the medication and notify the prescriber

explanation: Persistent vomiting contraindicates oral drug delivery because the patient cannot retain the medication, requiring an alternative route ordered by the physician. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: What body position is required for a patient receiving oral medications to prevent aspiration?
explanation: Sitting upright at a 60 to 90-degree angle uses gravity to guide the medication safely down the esophagus rather than toward the trachea. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is checking the patient's allergy band and chart mandatory before handing over oral pills?

options.A: To calculate the exact hepatic clearance rate
options.C: To verify the patient's insurance coverage
options.D: To determine the correct financial billing code

explanation: Cross-referencing allergy history protects the patient from administering substances that could trigger anaphylaxis or other dangerous immune responses. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: When should the nurse document that an oral medication has been swallowed by the patient?

options.B: Immediately after the patient takes the drug
options.C: At the end of the entire nursing shift

explanation: Documenting right away prevents accidental duplicate administration by other staff members and ensures an accurate clinical record. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: Which action represents the correct verification of the Right Patient identifier at the bedside?

options.A: Recognizing the patient's face from the morning report handover
options.B: Calling out the room number and waiting for someone to answer
options.C: Looking only at the chart face sheet kept at the nurses station
options.D: Asking the patient to state their full name while checking the wristband

explanation: Using two distinct identifiers, such as visual band check and active verbal confirmation, eliminates risks associated with misplaced patients or similar names. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: Which type of oral medication formulation must NEVER be crushed under any circumstances?
explanation: Crushing enteric coatings destroys the protective layer designed to prevent stomach irritation or drug destruction by gastric acid. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is the correct technique for measuring liquid medication into a graduated cup?

options.A: Read the base of the liquid meniscus at eye level on a flat surface
options.B: Hold the cup up to eye level and read the top of the fluid wave
options.C: Use a standard kitchen teaspoon for maximum patient familiarity
options.D: Fill the cup to the brim and pour out half into the sink

explanation: Placing the cup on a firm surface and viewing the fluid curve at eye level prevents parallax errors that lead to inaccurate dosing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: What should the nurse do if a patient is away from the bed when it is time for their scheduled oral medication?

options.A: Give the medication to a visiting family member to hold
options.B: Return the medication to the cart and secure it until the patient returns
options.C: Throw the medication into the trash and document refusal
options.D: Leave the pills neatly on the bedside table with a glass of water

explanation: Leaving medications unattended creates a high risk of omission, accidental ingestion by others, or tampering. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: A nurse prepares medications for two patients at the same time on a busy ward and mixes up their cups. What fundamental rule of administration was violated?

options.A: Using a graduated oral syringe for liquid volumes
options.B: Checking the medication label against the order twice
options.C: Preparing medications for only one patient at a time
options.D: Ensuring the patient is in a high Fowler's position

explanation: Preparing drugs sequentially for a single patient prevents cross-contamination, confusion, and administration errors between patients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: Why are elderly patients more vulnerable to adverse effects from standard doses of oral medications?

options.A: Age-related declines in hepatic and renal clearance
options.B: Increased production of gastric acid and digestive enzymes
options.C: Faster gastrointestinal motility reducing absorption time
options.D: Higher total body water percentage diluting the drug

explanation: Reduced organ function slows down the metabolism and excretion of drugs, causing them to accumulate in the bloodstream and increase toxicity risks. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: A mother insists on mixing her toddler's entire daily dose of bitter antibiotics into the child's morning milk bottle. What is the nurse's best response?

options.A: Tell her to double the dose if half the milk is left over
options.B: Advise against it because if the child refuses the milk, the full dose is lost
options.C: Suggest mixing it into a large pot of family soup instead
options.D: Encourage the practice as it guarantees complete compliance

explanation: Putting medication in a large volume of essential food or drink means that unfinished portions result in unknown, partial dosing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of post-administration monitoring after giving an oral drug?

options.A: To determine when the next nursing shift change occurs
options.B: To calculate the total financial cost of the hospital stay
options.C: To evaluate therapeutic efficacy and check for adverse reactions
options.D: To test the patient's long-term memory recall

explanation: Monitoring ensures the drug is working as intended and allows early detection of any unexpected side effects or allergic reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)

question: What action is required when a patient refuses a scheduled morning antihypertensive tablet?

options.A: Leave the medication on the bedside locker until they change their mind
options.B: Hide the pill in the patient's food so they take it unknowingly
options.C: Document the refusal with the stated reason and notify the prescriber
options.D: Force the patient to swallow the pill to maintain their blood pressure

explanation: Competent patients have the right to refuse treatment; nurses must document this transparently and report it to the medical team for alternative management. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)
